newsitem.title: GERMANY: Yeltsin sees Russia joining Paris club this year.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin sees Russia joining Paris club this year.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin said on Thursday that he expected Moscow to be admitted to the Paris club of sovereign lenders this year.
"I think that we should join the Paris club already in the current year," Yeltsin told a news conference after a meeting here with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
Yeltsin did not elaborate. His comments restated remarks he made in March when he said membership would make it easier to get better repayment terms on $37 billion in foreign debt owed to Moscow.
The cash mainly consists of loans extended under communism to lure a host of Third World countries into the Soviet Union's orbit.
French Prime Minister Alain Juppe said last week he would support Russia's entry into multilateral institutions -- including the Paris club -- as long as economic reforms progress.
Moscow has also taken steps to win Bonn's support to join the Paris club by putting in order the servicing of its debt to Germany -- which accounts for over half of its foreign debt.

The two countries last February signed a pact to reschedule 25 billion marks in Soviet-era debts over a period of 20 to 25 years. The debt agreement marked the bilateral implementation of a deal reached with the Paris club a year ago.

The deal was hailed at the time by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel as the last outstanding deal governing Soviet debts owed to Germany, and he said it opened the way for Russia to tap international capital markets again.
Hard on its heels came Russia's first mark-denominated Eurobond -- a seven-year, two billion mark issue -- raised in March.
Moscow had already issued its first $1 billion Eurobond last November, and is expected by bankers to return to the market with another dollar offering in June.
The Russian government has also said it was seeking to sign a deal this month with the International Monetary Fund covering financial plans for 1997.
The IMF has already delayed several tranches of a $10 billion, three-year facility because of poor tax receipts and both sides have been working on a statement of intent to cover the current year.
